title: Whose Image Is This?
objective: Students will read Jesus’ answer about the Tribute Penny as more than a ruling on taxes. The coin bears Caesar’s image, so it belongs to Caesar; every human person bears God’s image, so every person belongs to God. Students will connect Matthew 22:15–22 to Genesis 1:27 and to the Church’s teaching on the duties of citizens, and reflect on what it means to *give back to God* the life that carries his image.

objectives.why: Coins, flags and screens all ask for our loyalty every day. Jesus’ question gives us a way to tell what belongs to God.

materials: An image of the Tribute Penny (the exhibition page, or the coin on the student handout)
Any coin from a student’s pocket or purse
questions: What is the first thing you notice about the face on this coin?
If you were a faithful Jew in Jerusalem, how would it feel to carry a coin that called the emperor the son of a god?
The Tribute Penny sits beside the Shekel of Tyre, the coin that paid Judas. What do these two coins, side by side, say about money and loyalty?
Jesus asked his questioners to show him the coin. Why might it matter that they were the ones carrying it?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** find the Tribute Penny in Case 7, *Ministry and Passion*, and look for the inscription. Then walk to the Shekel of Tyre beside it — the coin that paid for the betrayal.
**Virtual visit:** the coin, its reverse and the full Gospel Timeline are online.

steps.title: Read a coin
script: Hold up an ordinary coin. *“Whose face is on this? What words are written on it? What is the coin claiming?”* Take answers: a president, a motto, a date, a country. Then: *“Every coin tells you who is in charge. Two thousand years ago, someone handed Jesus a coin and tried to trap him with it.”*

steps.purpose: Get students reading a coin as a message before the story begins.

steps.title: The trap
script: Read Matthew 22:15–22 aloud. Set out the trap: if Jesus says *pay the tax*, he sides with the occupying power and loses the crowd; if he says *don’t*, he can be reported to Rome as a rebel.

verse.text: “Show me the coin used for paying the tax.” They brought him a denarius, and he asked them, “Whose image is this? And whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they replied. Then he said to them, “So give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

steps.purpose: Understand the dilemma Jesus was put in.
students: What happens to Jesus if he says *yes*?

steps.title: The coin
script: Show the Tribute Penny. The face is Tiberius; the inscription calls him the son of a god; the reverse names him High Priest. For a faithful Jew this was not neutral money — it was an image claiming divine and religious authority.

coin.label: Case 7 · Ministry and Passion
coin.title: The Tribute Penny
body: The face is the emperor Tiberius. The inscription calls him *son of the divine Augustus*, and the reverse reads PONTIF MAXIM — *High Priest*. To a faithful Jew, the coin itself was a provocation.

steps.purpose: See why this coin was a provocation to a faithful Jew.
students: Read the words: PONTIF MAXIM means “High Priest”.
Who does this coin belong to?

steps.title: Whose image?
script: Jesus asks his questioners to produce the coin — and they can. *“Whose image is this? And whose inscription?”* The coin carries Caesar’s image, so give it back to Caesar. Then the turn: what carries *God’s* image? Read Genesis 1:27. St. Augustine and other early Christian writers drew exactly this line: Caesar looks for his image on his coin; God looks for his image in us.

verse.text: So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.

steps.purpose: Make the turn from the coin to the person.
students: Finish the sentence: *“I carry God’s image, so…”*

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels read the same passage and the same coin.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read the passage in short parts. Label the coin’s image and inscription, match each to Caesar or to God, and finish the sentence: *I carry God’s image, so…* Draw yourself as a coin stamped with God’s image.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Explain the trap and why Jesus’ answer escapes it. Compare the coin with Genesis 1:27 in a two-column chart, then write a paragraph on what *giving back to God* asks of a twelve-year-old today.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Write a structured reflection: is Jesus’ answer about taxes, about idolatry, or about the human person? Use the coin’s inscription, Genesis 1:27 and CCC 2242, and judge a modern case where obeying the state and obeying God might conflict.

steps.purpose: Practice the idea independently at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the same passage and the same coin.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen. For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now read a coin as evidence? Can you explain the trap, and how Jesus’ answer escapes it? Can you connect Caesar’s coin to God’s image in you? Can you judge when obedience to the state must give way to conscience?”* Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.

steps.title: Closing prayer
script: Ask students to hold a coin in an open hand. Pray together: *“Lord, the coin carries the image of the one who made it. We carry yours. Help us to give back to you what is yours — our time, our gifts, and our whole selves. Amen.”*
